--- title: "Splitting the data" description: "Training, validation and test data, how to keep a rare class in every part, why a random split is the wrong split for a marine survey, and what a rare class needs beyond the split." order: 7 categories: [data-preparation, validation, class-imbalance] --- ## A model must be tested on data it has not seen A model always looks good on the data it learned from; the only honest measure of how it will do on new stations is data it has never seen. [Prediction and explanation](../01-introduction/prediction-and-explanation.qmd) compared two models that way. This page shows how to hold data back, how to keep a rare class in every part, and why, for a marine survey, the rows held back must be chosen with more care than a random draw. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## Three roles for the data ::: {.diagram} ![Left: the three roles held-back data can play. Right: two ways to split a survey that visits each site several times. A random split puts visits to the same site on both sides; a split by site keeps each site whole.](img/split-roles.svg){fig-alt="Two panels. Three roles: training data, which the model learns from; validation data, used to choose between models; test data, used once to report the result. Two ways to split: four sites, A to D, each visited three times and drawn as three squares. In the random split one visit from every site is marked as test, so every test station's site is also in training. In the split by site all three visits to site D are test, so the test site is new to the model."} ::: - **Training data**: the model learns from it. - **Validation data**: used to *choose*, between models or between settings of one model. Choosing is a kind of learning, so it must not use the test data. - **Test data**: used once, at the end, to report how well the chosen model does. The validation role is the one most often skipped. Try eight models and report the best one's test score, and that score is the best of eight noisy numbers, which is too high. The test data answers "how good is this model?", never "which model is best?". When data is scarce, **cross-validation** takes the validation role by letting parts of the training data take turns; [Hyperparameter selection](../05-generalisation/hyperparameter-selection.qmd) covers it. Common splits keep 70 to 80% for training. The exact share is a trade-off between training the model well and measuring it precisely; how the rows are chosen matters far more. ## A random split is the starting point The cleaned survey (see [Missing values and outliers](missing-values-and-outliers.qmd)), split at random, three quarters for training: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() plain <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75) tibble(training = nrow(training(plain)), testing = nrow(testing(plain))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| training| testing| |--------:|-------:| | 600| 200|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit, train_test_split from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() plain_train, plain_test = train_test_split(survey, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) pd.DataFrame({"training": [len(plain_train)], "testing": [len(plain_test)]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | training | testing | |-----------:|----------:| | 600 | 200 | ::: ::: ::: ## Stratifying keeps a rare class in both parts The rare species is present at 5.1% of stations, 41 in all. A random split can easily leave very few of them in the test data. A **stratified** split (`strata =` in R, `stratify=` in Python) keeps the same share in both parts. Or it should: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) unstratified <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75) stratified <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75, strata = rare_species) share <- function(split) { tibble(train_pct = round(100 * mean(training(split)$rare_species == "yes"), 1), test_pct = round(100 * mean(testing(split)$rare_species == "yes"), 1)) } bind_rows(Unstratified = share(unstratified), Stratified = share(stratified), .id = "split") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|split | train_pct| test_pct| |:------------|---------:|--------:| |Unstratified | 4.7| 6.5| |Stratified | 6.0| 2.5|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} unstrat_train, unstrat_test = train_test_split( survey, train_size=0.75, random_state=2026) strat_train, strat_test = train_test_split( survey, train_size=0.75, random_state=2026, stratify=survey["rare_species"]) def share(frame): return round(100 * (frame["rare_species"] == "yes").mean(), 1) pd.DataFrame([ {"split": "Unstratified", "train_pct": share(unstrat_train), "test_pct": share(unstrat_test)}, {"split": "Stratified", "train_pct": share(strat_train), "test_pct": share(strat_test)}, ]) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | split | train_pct | test_pct | |:-------------|------------:|-----------:| | Unstratified | 5.2 | 5 | | Stratified | 5.2 | 5 | ::: ::: ::: In R the "stratified" split is no better than the plain one. `rsample` quietly merges any class smaller than its `pool` argument, 10% by default, so a class at 5.1% is not stratified at all, with no error. scikit-learn has no such threshold, so the Python tab is already balanced. Lowering `pool` fixes the R split: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(2026) properly <- initial_split(survey, prop = 0.75, strata = rare_species, pool = 0.01) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` #> Warning: Stratifying groups that make up 1% of the data may be statistically risky. #> ℹ Consider increasing `pool` to at least 0.1. ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} share(properly) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| train_pct| test_pct| |---------:|--------:| | 5| 5.5|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} # scikit-learn's stratify has no pooling step: it already split the rare class # directly, which the R tab needs pool = 0.01 to do. pd.DataFrame({"train_pct": [share(strat_train)], "test_pct": [share(strat_test)]}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | train_pct | test_pct | |------------:|-----------:| | 5.2 | 5 | ::: ::: ::: R now warns that the class is small, which is fair: 41 stations is thin ground to stratify on. The wider lesson: **check that a safeguard did what you asked**, by looking at the result rather than the code. ## Random is not independent A random split treats rows as interchangeable. Survey rows are not: visits to the same site are alike ([Observations and features](observations-and-features.qmd)). If one visit lands in training and another in test, the model has, in effect, already seen the test station. A **grouped split** keeps each site whole: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} grouped <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) sites_in_both <- function(split) { length(intersect(training(split)$site_id, testing(split)$site_id)) } tibble(split = c("Random", "By site"), sites_in_both = c(sites_in_both(plain), sites_in_both(grouped))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|split | sites_in_both| |:-------|-------------:| |Random | 120| |By site | 0|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) group_train, group_test = survey.iloc[train_rows], survey.iloc[test_rows] def sites_in_both(train, test): return len(set(train["site_id"]) & set(test["site_id"])) pd.DataFrame({ "split": ["Random", "By site"], "sites_in_both": [sites_in_both(plain_train, plain_test), sites_in_both(group_train, group_test)], }) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | split | sites_in_both | |:--------|----------------:| | Random | 123 | | By site | 0 | ::: ::: ::: Under the random split, 100% of the test stations sit at a site the model trained on. Whatever that test measures, it is not how well the model predicts a new place, which is what a habitat map is for. ## Split along what you will predict The two splits answer different questions: | Split | Question it answers | | --- | --- | | Random | How well does the model predict *another visit to a site already surveyed*? | | By site | How well does the model predict *a site never surveyed*? | Both are legitimate, but marine work usually claims the second while measuring the first. The rule is short: **split along whatever you intend to predict for.** New sites, split by site; next year, split by year; a new vessel, split by vessel. Splitting by site has a cost too: 160 sites give only about 40 test sites, so the test score is honest but uncertain. ## A rare class needs more than a split A rare outcome causes two problems beyond the split. **Accuracy misleads**: a model that always answers "absent" is right 95% of the time here, as [Exploring the data first](exploratory-analysis.qmd) found, so a model must be judged by how well it finds the rare class. And the **fitting is pulled towards the common class**, because getting that right is where the easy gains are. The usual remedies rebalance the training data: fewer rows of the common class (**down-sampling**), repeated rows of the rare one (**up-sampling**), made-up rare rows (**SMOTE**), or more weight on each rare row (**class weights**). The `themis` package provides them as recipe steps. Two conditions apply: - **Rebalance the training data only.** A rebalanced test set measures performance on a population that does not exist. `themis` steps skip new data automatically, but only inside a recipe, not when the table is balanced by hand. - **Expect the probabilities to shift.** A model trained on a 50/50 world predicts as if the species were common; [Class imbalance](../06-assumptions-limitations/class-imbalance.qmd) shows how far they shift. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Training data fits, validation data chooses, test data reports once. Choosing on the test data makes its score too high. - Stratify a rare class, and check the result: in R a class under 10% is silently not stratified unless `pool` is lowered. - Visits to the same site are alike, so a random split tests a model on places it has already seen. - Split along what you will predict for: new sites, new years, new vessels. - A rare class misleads accuracy and pulls the fit towards the common class; rebalance the training data only. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Run the random split with three different seeds and record the share of the rare species in each test set. How much does it move? 2. Fit a linear regression of `abundance` on depth, temperature and salinity under `initial_split()` and under `group_initial_split()`, and compare the test RMSE. The difference is what the random split was hiding. [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd) measures it with folds of stations, sites and blocks.
